scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. Probably a cruise, Japan or a trip to different countries in Europe I’ve never been to. It has about $2800 in it now. My brother has not been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially so he wouldn’t ask them for more help for that. Last week when he was complaining to my parents about it, they mentioned me and my vacation fund and said he could’ve been doing that all these years to be able to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. 3 days ago he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or Fall. He said since I won’t need it for another 2 years it’s plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do yet always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I do not pay rent either, which is why I have been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone and uni fees). He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

Borrowing it to your brother—especially someone who’s historically struggled with money—would be **self-sabotaging**. Even if he promises to pay you back, his track record suggests this is unlikely to happen in time. #### **2. He’s Not in a Position to Repay** - He makes **about as much as you** but still struggles financially. - He **doesn’t pay rent** (unlike you, who covers your own expenses). - He’s **horrible with money**—his past behavior suggests he’ll either: - Take longer than expected to pay you back, or - Not pay you back at all. - Even if he could, **$2,800 is a significant sum** for someone who’s already in a tight spot. #### **3. His Arguments Are Weak & Self-Serving** - **"I had to work harder than you"** → This is **not a valid financial reason** to borrow your money. Hardship doesn’t mean you should exploit someone else’s savings. - **"Mom and Dad spoiled you"** → This is **gaslighting**. Your parents **did not** spoil you—they let you **earn and save** your own money. Meanwhile, they’ve been supporting him financially for years. - **"You got to go on trips with them more"** → This is **emotional manipulation**. You’re not obligated to fund his vacations just because you had different childhood experiences. #### **4. The Emotional & Psychological Toll** - You’re **already stressed about school**—why add financial stress by potentially losing your savings? - If he **doesn’t pay you back**, you’ll feel **resentful, used, and taken advantage of**. - If he **does pay you back late**, you’ll still feel **exploited** because he took your money in the first place. --- ### **What You Could Do Instead:** 1. **Set a Firm Boundary** - *"I’m not lending you money because I don’t trust you to pay it back on time. If you want to save for a trip, you’ll have to do it yourself."* - **Do not negotiate.** If he keeps asking, **repeat the same thing politely but firmly.** 2. **Make Him Earn It (If You Feel Sympathetic)** - If you *really* want to help, you could say: *"If you want to go to Japan, save up yourself. But if you need help, I’ll help you find a side job to earn the money."* - This forces him to **take responsibility** rather than relying on you. 3. **Document the Conversation (If Needed)** - If he **keeps pressuring you**, you can say: *"I’ve already said no, and I don’t want to discuss this further."* - If he **threatens or guilt-trips you**, you can **record the conversation** (if legal in your country) as proof. 4. **Protect Your Fund** - If he **still tries to borrow**, you can: - **Freeze the account** (if it’s digital). - **Keep the money in a separate account** where he can’t access it. - **Tell your parents** (if they’re supportive) to help enforce the boundary. --- ### **Final Verdict:** **You are absolutely not AITA.** You’re being **self-respecting, financially responsible, and realistic** about his character. **Your money is yours to save for your own dreams**, not to fund someone else’s impulsive decisions. If he **can’t respect that**, then he doesn’t deserve your help—**even if he’s family**. **Boundaries are healthy**, and **you’re not obligated to enable his financial irresponsibility**. Would you like help drafting a **stronger response** if he keeps pushing?
